images.notes: Hand-coloured fire/real-estate atlas detail covering the whole 1600 and 1700 blocks of Prairie between 16th St (top/north) and 18th St, with the Illinois Central tracks, '16th St. Station I.C.R.R.' and the lakeshore: pink = brick, yellow = frame, brown = stone (Pullman house at 18th St). Lot numbers, subdivision names, frontages and outbuildings (crossed = stables) are legible. Shows NO through 17th Street between Indiana and the lake — the 1600 and 1700 blocks are continuous on both sides of Prairie, which matters for siting 1638/1700 and 1637/1701. The blue arrow marks the yellow (frame) Tyrrell/Walker house at 1720; the 1702 Staples/Harvey house (pre-1899) is still shown, so the plate pre-dates the 1700/1706 townhouses. Compare with project file maps/originals/robinson-1886-north-block.jpg (likely the same plate).

images.notes: Modern compiled map of building footprints 16th–22nd Streets (Indiana to the IC) with 1886 occupants from directories and social registers, 100-ft scale bar. For the 1600–1700 blocks it lists: 1600 John G. Shortall; 1608 H. L. Frank; 1616 W. R. Stirling; 1620 Robert H. Law and Dr Lyman Ware; 1628 B. M. and Maurice Einstein; 1630 Peter Brust (foreman — the small house); 1638 Robert B. Gregory; 1702 T. W. Harvey; 1712 Albert Sturges; 1720 Ella Walker; 1736 Hugh and Hugh J. (Jr.) McBirney; east side 1619 Joseph L. McBirney; 1621 John Hamline; 1623 Granger Farwell; 1637 Jesse Spalding; 1701 W. G. Hibbard; 1709 Martha Kellogg; 1721 Wirt Dexter; 1729 Pullman; 16th Street IC station. No building is drawn at 1635 (supports Forsyth house gone by 1886) and none at 1609–1611 beyond small outlines — check against the Robinson original. Footprints appear derived from the 1886 Robinson atlas; use as an index, not as primary geometry. Also confirms that in 1886 Hugh J. McBirney lived with his father at 1736 (so his 1890 Burling & Whitehouse house was a new address — 1625 by 1904).

images.notes: Construction photo by George Glessner: the brick shell of the Shepley, Rutan & Coolidge townhouses with slate mansard and pedimented dormers in place, window openings still unglazed, a builder's shed and lumber in the front yard; stone string course, keystoned first-floor arches and a sign board over the door. At left a three-storey brick/stone house with a two-storey bay and a hooded doorway (= 1708, the house immediately south; Thorne residence by 1911 — see the Christmas-tree photograph captioned 1708/1706/1700; 1911 Sanborn: 1708 3-storey brick dwelling); at right the steep-gabled Gothic Revival house with porch (1638, Gregory — the 1600 and 1700 blocks were not separated by a through 17th Street). Gives the exact massing and materials (red brick, light stone trim) of the pair as finished c.1902 and shows the neighbours in 1901.

images.notes: The Shepley, Rutan & Coolidge Georgian Revival double townhouse built 1901–02 for the Glessner children: a continuous three-storey dark-brick block under a slate mansard with pedimented dormers and a wooden roof balustrade (Chinese-Chippendale pattern); stone keystoned flat-arched windows on the second floor, round-arched first-floor windows with iron balconettes; two mirror-image columned entrance porticoes with balconies above, at the outer ends; iron area railings. At the right edge the steep-gabled Gothic Revival house with pointed windows = 1638 (Gregory), immediately north — the 1600 and 1700 blocks were continuous (no through 17th Street; see the atlas crop record). At left a rusticated stone-trimmed three-storey neighbour = 1708 (James Ward Thorne residence by 1911; cf. the 'Christmas tree' photograph, which captions the same three houses as 1708, 1706, 1700). Caption labels left = 1706, right = 1700 (north unit), consistent with a view from the east. The same photograph appears (sepia, sharper) on the Glessner House blog post 'Kodak plant demolition begins' (2015-03-10) captioned 'Glessner townhouses, 1700-1706 S. Prairie Avenue, Shepley, Rutan & Coolidge, architects'. Strong evidence for the 1904 appearance; townhouses demolished 1954 for the Kodak plant expansion.

images.notes: Hand-drawn memory map of Prairie Avenue between (unnamed) 16th St and Glessner's corner, Lake Michigan and the IC tracks at top (east). East side, north→south: Hamline, Farwell, McBirney, Forsyth, Hibbard, Hibbard, Williams, Dexter, Pullman; then across 18th St: Massacre Tree & Monument, Pullman Park, Kimball, Buckingham, Casselberry. West side north→south: Shortall, Anderson, Stirling, Hibbard, Einstein, Johnstone, Gregory, Harvey, Sturges, Walker, Otis; 18th St; Glessner. Not to scale and conflates periods (Williams house gone c.1882, Kimball 1890s) — use as an owner-sequence/lot-order aid, not geometry. Note the second 'Hibbard' on the east side (1637, rented by Hibbard 1866) and 'Gregory' at 1638.

images.notes: The John W. Roberts Gothic Revival ('Hudson River Gothic') house: steep front gable with crocketed finial and oculus, paired pointed-arch windows with hood moulds, a canted ground-floor bay with pointed lights, a polygonal corner tower with pointed windows and a tall conical/pyramidal slate roof, a Gothic entrance porch with pierced brackets over a stoop, a lower wing at left, and gate piers with an iron fence. Block-by-block perspective line drawing with printed house numbers on the curb line: 1702, 1712, 1720, 1726, 1730, 1736, '18th St.', 1800 (Glessner, with its arched entry and 18th-Street wall), 1808, 1812. Drawn c.1892–93: 1702 here is the pre-Glessner-Lee-townhouse house (pa-1702-43, demolished before 1904) and 1726 is the early house later replaced, so for 1904 this is evidence of the earlier generation at those two lots; 1720, 1736, 1800–1812 are the buildings standing in 1904. Diagrammatic — façades are simplified and proportions not reliable for measurement; treat as a numbered sequence/massing guide.

images.notes: KEY FIND — the only located image of Arthur Little's 1889 Colonial Revival front addition that brought the Dexter house up nearly to the lot line (the frame 1863 house survived behind it). Shows a three-storey light-coloured brick (or painted) block with a bowed (swell) centre bay rising full height, shuttered sash windows, iron balconettes on the first floor, a two-column entrance porch with a balustraded balcony above, a modillioned cornice and a balustraded parapet over the roof, a tall chimney; at the left rear the older gabled frame block with bay windows; at right edge the mansard and cresting of the Pullman house. Low stone kerb wall and young elms along the sidewalk. This is the 1904 frontage of 1721 (per AIC street field '1721 S. Prairie Ave.'; later owner moved the addition back — after 1904). The 1911 Sanborn's 'two curved Prairie-facing bays' at 1719 may record the relocated block.

images.notes: Glass negative ('286' on negative; holder note 'Prarie Avenue'). Date bracket from Detroit Catalogue J (1901); the Fort Dearborn Massacre monument (erected 1893) is visible at the far right end of 18th Street, so the view is 1893 or later. The best in-period full view of the Pullman house's west (Prairie) and south (18th St) fronts: three-storey ashlar Second Empire block with mansard, iron roof cresting, pedimented dormers, ivy-covered walls, columned entrance porch on Prairie, corner/side porch on 18th, low stone-capped wall with piers along both sidewalks, lamp posts, young elms on parkway, unpaved/macadam roadway with stone crosswalk slabs and a carriage at the 18th St kerb. At the left edge, the neighbouring house to the north (1721 Prairie, Wirt Dexter house, identification by position) shows a broad columned front porch, gabled dormers and tall chimneys — useful for the Dexter house's 1889 Arthur Little front. Leafless trees: autumn/spring.

The Glessner House blog identifies the top-centre street vignette as 'Prairie Avenue looking southwest at 18th Street' (the pre-Glessner corner) — see a18-gh-landowner-1874-glessner-site; the vignette captioned 'Louis Wahl' is 2026 Prairie.

images.notes: KEY NEAR-1904 STREET VIEW. Looking south along the west sidewalk from 18th Street: Glessner's granite north-east corner and the low stone coping/curb walls of its parkway at right, then the stepped stoops, bays and mansard roofs of 1808, 1812, 1816 and beyond receding south; a double row of mature elms in the parkway, wide unpaved/macadam carriageway at left, gas lamp posts. Inscribed "9974 J.W.T." The tree size (much larger than in the c. 1888 Glessner photo) puts it in the late 1890s–1900s — the closest dated-type view to 1904 for the west side of the 1800 block. A second print is in the D. G. Lowe collection (mqc 75920); the same view was issued as a coloured postcard postmarked 1908 (st-ghm-postcard-1908-prairie-south-at-18th) and reproduced in the 1973 Landmarks Commission report. RBA caption/notes: Description: Taylor #9974. Looking south from 18th St.

Possible source: William Tyre's Chicago's Historic Prairie Avenue (Arcadia, 2008) pp. 44–45 reproduces 'Bird's-Eye Views and Guide to Chicago', Rand McNally 1898, with renderings in two rows that include 1936, 1912, 1906, 1900 and 1901, 1905, 1919, 1923, 1945 (per the AIC Ryerson & Burnham 'Building Index of Selected Chicago Architectural Monographs', 2014) — if this blog image is that plate it dates from 1898 (in-period). Not the same as the 1893 perspective strips (IA randmcnallycosbi00lawr p.269). Unconfirmed; the 1898 edition was not found online this session.

images.notes: Contemporary (1883–84) description of the house exterior and plan — the best period text for the 1904 model: 'red pressed brick, with trimmings of light sandstone, three stories in height, with main entrance in the center of the west front, at the head of a broad flight of granite steps, a high porte-cochère on the northern side, and a fine large conservatory on the southern. images.notes: Large clear photograph of the Van Osdel–designed Tucker/Byron L. Smith house on the NW corner of 22nd: dark brick with stone bands, three tall conical-roofed round/polygonal corner towers with cresting and finials, Gothic gabled dormers, clustered chimneys; tall iron picket fence on brick piers with ball finials; an iron-and-glass arched porte-cochère/entrance canopy on the 22nd Street (south) side. At right (north) a rough-faced stone house with a conical-roofed rounded bay — very probably 2130 Murdoch (H. I. Cobb, 1890) — and beyond it a long three-storey brick row. Overhead trolley wires and rails in 22nd Street, a cast-iron street lamp at right, a man with a bicycle. Strong 1904 evidence: shows the corner, the fence, the canopy and the trolley wires; date window inferred c. 1890–1911. Compared with the pre-1881 Greene stereograph, the towers here carry tall conical slate roofs — a later remodelling, after 1890 (the cresting-crowned towers still stood next to the 1890 Murdoch house in a20-glessner-vanosdel-2140-photo); whether 1904 had spires or cresting is unresolved — date this photo before choosing. The 1898 Van Osdel book plate (a20-aic-quarter-century-tucker-residence) still shows the cresting state, which (if the photo was current in 1898) would put the spires after 1898.

images.title: National Register nomination, Henry B. Clarke House, 4526 South Wabash Avenue (before 1872, 16th and Michigan), with 'Henry B. Clarke House Amendment: Relocation' (2000)
images.date: original nomination c.1970–71 (Commission on Chicago Historical and Architectural Landmarks); amendment prepared August 23, 2000
images.creator: Susan Benjamin, Commission on Chicago Historical and Architectural Landmarks (1970s form); City of Chicago Dept. of Cultural Affairs (2000 amendment)

images.found_via: IA full-text search '"Chrimes" "Wabash avenue" oldest house' → item file list
images.notes: Original form (read in OCR): 13-room two-storey frame house of rough-hewn oak, raised basement, 'Italian Victorian cupola, added after construction'; tall narrow main-floor windows, small 'eyebrow' windows upstairs; low-pitched front gable; 'originally … a typical Greek Revival columned portico'; moved 1872 by John Chrimes to 4526 S. Wabash; owner since 1941 St Paul Church of God in Christ. Bibliography lists Tribune 'The Clarke House: Henry B. Clarke's Ten Thousand Dollar House' (26 May 1872) and 'Discovery of Interesting Papers' (9 June 1872), plus 1939–1969 'oldest house' articles. 2000 amendment: footprint 42.44 × 47.37 ft, east facade, raised portico 31 × 9.5 ft (restored 1980 from a c.1855 daguerreotype in the Chicago Historical Society); HABS 1935 found most window mouldings, pilasters, shutters and the portico modified/removed; four corner pilasters, two roofline pediments and the cupola remained; neither the 1836 nor the 1872 foundation survives. Includes a site plan and floor plans of the house at 1827 S. Indiana (pp. 16–18) and a mid-20th-century photograph (p. 24). For 1904: the house stood at 4526 Wabash with cupola, no portico.

images.creator: Ryerson & Burnham Libraries, Art Institute of Chicago

images.notes: Descriptions: Rees house (1888) — 'three stories and an attic … of Bedford stone that has been completely smoothed … on a rusticated base. A great, simple arch with over-sized voussoirs shelters the entrance. To its south, a curved bay stands two stories and ends in a semicircular copper roof. A group of five arched windows light the third floor and a steep gable with a single arched window rises to a finial.' Murdoch house (1890) — random ashlar of smooth stone on a battered foundation, corner porch on paired columns with trabeated openings, gable to the side yard, a semicircular-plan section rising to a conical roof above the third storey, low-relief frieze. ADDRESS CONFLICT: the older AIC page calls it 'Murdock … 2130 S. Calumet Ave., one block east of Prairie', the 1890–99 page '2130 S. Prairie'; Chicagology, the HMDB marker and the Robinson 1886 empty lot support Prairie. Also Gorton (2120 Prairie): Burnham & Root 1877 house for O. W. Clapp, Cobb music-room addition for F. S. Gorton (c.1891–96, demolished 1950). No Murdoch image in the catalogue; the only image found is as the neighbour in the 2140 photographs.

images.notes: 62-page PDF. Answers the 'HABS?' question: no HABS documentation is cited; the house is an NRHP individual listing (1999) and a Chicago Landmark (5 Feb 1998, per Wikipedia). Description: c.1870 three-storey Second Empire house of orange-rust brick (walls four courses thick) on an Indiana limestone raised basement, stone window hoods with incised floral ornament and large keystones, front (EAST) elevation in three zones; a limestone Queen Anne entry verandah/porch and front steps added c.1880–1900; a two-storey pressed-copper bay with pyramidal copper roof at the southeast corner added c.1880s–early 1890s (compared with the c.1890 copper bay on the Kimball house); alley to the west; a later warehouse/cooler addition at the NW. So in 1904 the house had its copper bay and stone porch (both pre-1904) but not the 20th-c. warehouse additions. Occupied by the Kohn family from 1874 for 34 years (to c.1908).

images.title: National Register of Historic Places Inventory–Nomination Form: 2nd Presbyterian Church, 1936 S. Michigan Av. (NRIS 74000754)
images.creator: Thomas G. Yanul and Paul E. Sprague, Illinois Historic Structures Survey
images.repository: U.S. National Archives (NARA), RG 79 National Park Service — National Register nomination files (digitized)
images.rights_basis: Government-hosted nomination; photographs/drawings by state survey staff and photographers — reuse rights not established
images.found_via: NRIS number in HABS IL-328 record; NARA S3 PDF read in full (26 pp.)
images.notes: Key text for the 1904 church. Lot 109'×171' at NW corner of Cullerton (20th) and Michigan; east & south facades of mottled bituminous ('fairy') limestone, north & west of Chicago common brick; gable roof; nave runs E–W with the parish house at right angles (abbreviated T); main entry on the east; balconies on E, N, S. Nave 95 ft long, 60 ft high, 75 ft wide incl. aisles. History: Renwick & Sands, completed 1874; spring 1900 fire gutted the nave; Shaw's rebuild completed 1901. EXTERIOR CHANGES MADE IN THE 1900–01 REBUILD (i.e. the 1904 state differs from Renwick's drawings): clerestory windows changed from pointed arches to a rectilinear grouping; the traditional rose window replaced by an ogee-shaped window; roof ridge LOWERED. Only later change: removal of the tower's hipped roof after storm damage in 1959 — so in 1904 the SE tower carried a hipped roof. Large Tiffany window over the main Michigan Avenue entry (4½ tons). Bibliography cites House Beautiful v.17 no.1 (Dec. 1904) — a contemporary illustrated article (lead).

Cornerstone 21 Sept 1872; first services Jan 1873 (Sunday-school room) and 30 Nov 1873 (sanctuary); BELL TOWER COMPLETED 1884. 'The tower was originally topped by a graceful spire with a tall, slender finial, but these were lost due to wind damage in 1929' (the 1974 NRHP form instead says the tower's hipped roof was removed after a 1959 storm — conflict to resolve with dated photographs; either way the 1904 tower had a tall roof/spire). Church ~60 ft high; exterior 110 × 168 ft; nave about 72 × 116 ft; seats ~1,200. Fire of 9 March 1900 destroyed the roof and much of the nave interior; Shaw's rebuild LOWERED and flattened the nave roof (original 'more sharply pitched and its peak considerably higher'), and the east-wall rose window (La Farge round mosaic, destroyed 1900) was replaced. Exterior description: four-storey square tower with corner buttresses, open belfry with paired pointed arches and angel figures, corner gargoyles; central Gothic portal with head of Christ; five lancets and a large window under the gable with symbols of the Evangelists; north buttress pinnacle 'once topped by a tall finial'; north and south walls with three rows of windows (copper-framed opalescent clerestory, six large pointed windows, small windows below); north side brick; west transverse section with wheel window and copper oriel; mottled bituminous limestone laid in banded stringcourses. Original interior: tall Gothic arches on slender cast-iron columns, light and airy.

images.notes: Coarse-screen halftone captioned 'Shirley T. High Residence'. Shows a three-storey dark brick house with a steep front gable, a round corner tower with conical roof at left, arched entrance up a stone stoop, tall chimney, and a broad north side wing with a second gable; picket fence at right. This form is Queen Anne/Richardsonian of the 1880s — consistent with J. L. High's 1886 purchase and 1887 rear addition (Inter Ocean 20 Aug 1887 permit, quoted) or a rebuild; it is not obviously the late-1870s Adams house. Date unknown (Chicagology file name '1930' is not a holder date; Shirley T. High was James L. High's son) — period left unset. Needs source identification before use for 1904. Lead: the 1973 Commission report bibliography cites John Drury, 'Old Chicago Houses: Prairie Avenue Survivor,' Chicago Daily News, 19 Jan 1940 (Adams/High House); its text says the house was then still occupied by Maj. Shirley T. High (65) and was a '2½-story, 16-room residence … built in the late 1870s by Benjamin Adams … sold in 1886 to Major High's father … for $40,000'. The halftone with the 'Shirley T. High Residence' caption is plausibly from that 1940 article — unverified.
